subject: Copywriting
title: Dollar Shave Club: Our Blades Are Great
description: One-minute skill: Dollar Shave Club: Our Blades Are Great.

hook.text: A cheeky YouTube video in 2012 declared 'Our Blades Are F***ing Great.' Humor, honesty, and $1 razors built a $1B brand.

buildup.text: Michael Dubin shot the launch video for $4,500. It got 12,000 orders in 48 hours.

discovery.text: The slogan worked because it said what everyone was thinking: razor blades are overpriced—and ours are genuinely great.

twist.text: Gillette, the $10B incumbent, initially ignored them. By the time Gillette responded, DSC had 15% of the US market.

climax.text: Unilever bought Dollar Shave Club for $1 billion in 2016. A slogan and a video disrupted a century-old industry.

punchline.text: $4,500 video, $1B exit. Great copy beats great budgets.

details.whyItMatters: This slogan shows that challenger brands can win with personality alone. When incumbent messaging is polished and generic, raw honesty becomes the most disruptive creative strategy.
takeaways: The viral launch video cost $4,500 and generated millions of views
Profanity signaled authenticity against corporate razor marketing
Unilever acquired Dollar Shave Club for $1 billion in 2016

faq.question: Why did profanity work for Dollar Shave Club's slogan?
faq.answer: Gillette and Schick used sterile, aspirational language. Dollar Shave Club's profanity felt like a friend recommending something real. The swearing signaled: 'We're not a corporation — we're one of you.' This authenticity was the core differentiator.

faq.question: Can irreverent slogans work for any brand?
faq.answer: No. Irreverence works for challenger brands targeting consumers frustrated with the status quo. A luxury brand or a healthcare provider using profanity would undermine trust. The key is matching tone to audience expectations and brand position.
